passage: Diary, day 6 as monitor!! Ma'am gave me the register and the duster cupboard key, and honestly the class runs better now. I made everyone line up for water by roll number. When I say 'silence' they actually go silent. It's kind of amazing. Yusuf complained that the roll-number line is stupid because the last people never get time to drink before the bell. I told him monitors decide, not him. I also wrote Kavitha's name down for talking, even though she was only asking for a pen. Rules are rules. I don't know why Farah said 'you've changed' in a snarky voice at lunch. I'm the same Reena. I'm just in charge now. Tomorrow I'm making a seating chart. — Reena

passage: When the headmaster of the Sonpur high school chose Anand, fifteen, to run the cycle stand, he gave him a whistle and a notebook. By the second week Anand walked differently, slower, with the whistle swinging. He made the Class 8 kids park at the far end in the mud, while his friends got the shade under the neem tree. When Disha pointed out that her chain kept clogging with mud there, he didn't look up from the notebook. "Complaints in writing," he said, and his friends laughed. Anand liked the sound of that line. He liked the way small boys stepped aside for him. He barely noticed that Disha, who used to share her guava with him at recess, had started eating with other people.

qa.q: What did the headmaster give Anand?
qa.a: The headmaster gave him a whistle and a notebook.

qa.q: What does Anand's slower walk with the whistle swinging suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests Anand feels important and is enjoying the power the job gives him.

qa.q: What turning point could make Anand rethink the cycle stand, and what might he change?
qa.a: Noticing that Disha no longer eats with him could jolt Anand; he could share the shady spots fairly and actually listen to her problem with the mud.

qa.q: How does Disha experience Anand's new role?
qa.a: Disha feels brushed off, since he didn't even look up when she raised a real problem, and she has quietly moved away from their friendship.

grounding: Shows a teenager given charge of a cycle stand who starts favouring friends, enjoying deference and ignoring a peer's complaint.

passage: When Coach Lind made Oskar captain of the under-sixteen handball team in Gothenburg, he got an armband and the keys to the ball cupboard. By the third week he was a different player. He changed Tuesday practice to seven in the morning without asking anyone, because it suited his piano lessons. He made the younger boys collect all the balls while he practised penalties. When Sofia said that the new time meant she had to skip breakfast and cycle in the dark, Oskar didn't even stop bouncing the ball. "Captain decides. If you want to play, you come." A couple of the boys laughed. Oskar liked that, and liked how people moved when he pointed. He didn't notice that Sofia had stopped passing to him in practice.

qa.q: Why did Oskar move Tuesday practice to seven in the morning?
qa.a: Because it suited his piano lessons.

qa.q: How does Oskar feel about being obeyed, and what shows it?
qa.a: He enjoys being obeyed, liking how the boys laughed at his line and how people moved when he pointed.

qa.q: What could Oskar have done when Sofia raised her problem?
qa.a: He could have stopped, listened, and asked the whole team which practice time worked, instead of dismissing her.

qa.q: How does Sofia see Oskar's captaincy?
qa.a: She sees a captain who ignores her needs, skipping breakfast and cycling in the dark, and her not passing to him shows she has lost trust in him.

grounding: A teenage boy made captain starts bossing teammates, enjoys being obeyed and brushes off a complaint, caring only about his own schedule.

passage: The school library had a new prefect badge, and Aparna, fourteen, wore it pinned exactly in the centre of her pocket. At first she was helpful. By the second month, the library felt like her room. She moved the Class 7 students to the hard benches by the window so her friends could have the soft chairs. She started fining people a rupee for whispering, even when they were asking where a book was. When Akash said the fine was unfair because the librarian had never charged anything, Aparna tapped the badge. "The librarian put me in charge." She wrote his name in her notebook. Watching him leave, she felt a small satisfying click, like a door shutting. She didn't think about why fewer students came in at lunch.

qa.q: What did Aparna start fining people for?
qa.a: She started fining people a rupee for whispering.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she wrote Akash's name in her notebook?
qa.a: She felt a small satisfying click, which shows she enjoyed her power more than caring about his point.

qa.q: What could Aparna do if she wanted the library to feel fair again?
qa.a: She could ask the librarian and the students what the rules should be, drop the fine and share the soft chairs instead of keeping them for friends.

qa.q: How might the Class 7 students see the library now?
qa.a: They may feel pushed aside and unwelcome, which could explain why fewer students come in at lunch.

grounding: A teenage library prefect grows bossy with her small authority, enjoys being obeyed and dismisses a fair complaint.

passage: In class nine I was made class monitor, and I'm not proud of what happened next. I'm Yusuf. At first I just wrote names on the board when people talked. Then I started liking it. Liking how people went quiet when I stood up. I made my friends carry my bag, and I wrote down Tanuja's name every day because she argued with me. When she said, "You're not even fair, you talk too," I told her monitors don't have to follow the rules. I laughed at her in front of everyone. I didn't notice I'd stopped listening to anyone. My goal was a quiet class and a good report from Ma'am; that's all I could see. It was only when Tanuja cried in the corridor that I stopped and thought, when did I become this guy?

qa.q: Whose name did Yusuf write down every day?
qa.a: He wrote down Tanuja's name every day.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling as he started liking being monitor?
qa.a: Yusuf felt a pleasurable sense of power, enjoying how people went quiet, which slowly made him stop caring how others felt.

qa.q: What could Yusuf have done differently as monitor?
qa.a: He could have listened to complaints like Tanuja's and followed the same rules, using the role to keep things fair rather than to be obeyed.

qa.q: How did Tanuja experience Yusuf's time as monitor?
qa.a: Tanuja felt unfairly targeted and humiliated, until she cried in the corridor.

grounding: A teenager made class monitor starts bossing peers, enjoying being obeyed and dismissing complaints, as power narrows his attention.

PE teacher's note, Friday.
Arohi (class ten) was made football captain three weeks ago. At first she was great: organised, encouraging. This week I've watched a change. She decides every drill herself, shouts at players who question her, and made Swati run extra laps for "attitude" when Swati only asked why they weren't practising penalties. When two girls came to complain, Arohi rolled her eyes and walked off. She seems to enjoy being obeyed and to hear only her own plan. I don't think she sees it. Today I pulled her aside, told her what I'd noticed, and asked her to hold a five-minute team huddle after each session where anyone can speak. She was defensive but agreed. I'll watch Monday's practice.

qa.a: Arohi made Swati run extra laps for "attitude" when Swati only asked why they weren't practising penalties.

qa.q: What does Arohi's eye-roll at the complaining girls suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests Arohi felt annoyed and dismissive, enjoying her power and not wanting her plans questioned.

qa.q: Why is the five-minute team huddle a good idea?
qa.a: It gives players a regular chance to be heard, which pushes Arohi to pay attention to others' views instead of only her own goals.

qa.q: How might Swati feel about running extra laps for asking a question?
qa.a: Swati likely felt humiliated and resentful, punished for a fair question.

grounding: A teenage team captain starts bossing peers, enjoys being obeyed and dismisses complaints, as a teacher notices her attention narrowing.

passage:
In the small hill school near Gangtok, Pema was made class monitor in June. The first week she was kind. By July, she stood at the front with the register and a ruler.
"Jomon, names on the board for talking."
"I was asking for a pencil."
"Tell it to the teacher."
She liked how the room went quiet when she lifted the ruler. She wrote names for whispering, for laughing, even for dropping a tiffin box.
When Jomon said, "You used to talk more than anyone," she only wrote his name again.
At home she told her Ama, "They listen to me now." She didn't mention that nobody sat with her at lunch any more.

qa.q: When was Pema made class monitor?
qa.a: She was made class monitor in June.

qa.q: How does Pema feel when the room goes quiet as she lifts the ruler?
qa.a: She feels powerful and pleased, enjoying being obeyed.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help Pema?
qa.a: She stopped listening to her classmates; asking them how she's doing, and hearing reasons like the pencil, would help.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Pema now?
qa.a: Jomon feels annoyed and let down, since the girl who used to talk more than anyone now punishes him for asking for a pencil.

grounding: Shows a teenager made class monitor starting to boss classmates, enjoying obedience and dismissing complaints.

passage:
At the international school in Singapore, Hana was made captain of the swim team at fifteen. She was proud, and at first she worked hard for everyone.
Soon she was changing the relay order without asking. When Rafael said he swam better in the second leg, she said, "I decide that now." When two juniors complained that practice ran into their exam revision, she rolled her eyes. She only thought about the trophy.
At the next meet, Rafael swam where she put him and came in slow. The team lost by a second.
In the changing room nobody spoke to her. Hana told herself they were just sore losers.

qa.q: How old was Hana when she was made captain?
qa.a: She was made captain at fifteen.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she told herself the others were sore losers?
qa.a: She felt defensive and hurt, not wanting to see how her choices had upset the team.

qa.q: What could Hana do after the meet?
qa.a: She could ask the team, including Rafael and the juniors, what they think, and set the relay order together.

qa.q: What was it like for Rafael to swim where Hana put him?
qa.a: Rafael felt ignored and frustrated, knowing he swam better in the second leg but had no say.

grounding: Shows a teenager made team captain who starts deciding alone, enjoying being obeyed and ignoring others' views, with a cost to the team.

passage: You asked about being head girl. Honestly? I'm Minakshi, seventeen, and it changed me faster than I'd like to admit. In the first month I loved it: teachers calling me by name, juniors going quiet when I walked in. I started telling people how to line up, what to wear for assemblies, even how to speak to me. When the Class 8 kids complained about losing their lunch-break football for my discipline drive, I told them to stop whining. I didn't notice I'd stopped asking anyone anything. Then my best friend Sangeeta said, in the canteen, 'You talk to us like we're files now.' That stung. I went home and read back my messages from that month. She was right. Every message was an order.

qa.q: What did the Class 8 kids lose because of the discipline drive?
qa.a: Their lunch-break football.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when Sangeeta said 'You talk to us like we're files now'?
qa.a: Minakshi felt stung and hurt, then uneasy on seeing the orders in the old messages.

qa.q: What could Minakshi change after reading back the messages?
qa.a: Start asking juniors for their views and give back the football break, so the role serves people rather than control.

qa.q: How might the Class 8 kids see their head girl?
qa.a: They likely see her as bossy and unfair, having their football taken and their complaints dismissed.

grounding: A teenage head girl describes how a little power made her bossy and dismissive until a friend named it.
